title: Comparisons and logic: conditions as testable contracts
lead: Check a range with two conditions and distinguish “and” from “or”.
why: A condition can do more than answer yes or no: its order can protect an invalid operation. Short-circuiting follows exact built-in && and || rules rather than compiler intuition.
objectives: Express a range as two comparisons joined by &&.
Place a divisor guard before a dangerous expression.
prerequisites: bool, arithmetic, and mixed signed/unsigned from the previous lessons.
Splitting a computation into named stages. A complete if/else or loops course is unnecessary here.

concepts.definition: Here, a bool expression describing a property to check.
Built-in && is true when both operands are true; the right operand is skipped when the left is false.
Built-in || is true when at least one operand is true; the right operand is skipped when the left is true.
! reverses true and false after converting the operand to bool.
Skipping the right operand when the left already determines a built-in logical expression’s result.

sections.title: A comparison is a value, not assignment
paragraphs: score >= 0 produces bool. == compares equality and != inequality; a single = in assignment changes an object. score = 0 can be valid C++ inside a larger expression, but it is not an equality check. Inspect meaning even after a successful build.

Identify operand types first. As seen previously, int and unsigned int can change the expected meaning of a negative comparison. Our ranges use matching ints so that logic is studied without hidden mixed-sign conversions.

sections.title: A range is not a mathematical comparison chain
paragraphs: C++ 0 <= score <= 100 does not express two simultaneous bounds. First 0 <= score produces bool, which is then compared with 100. For the resulting 0 or 1, that second comparison is true even when score is invalid.

Use score >= 0 && score <= 100. One comparison checks the lower bound and one the upper; both must hold. Name the result validScore when useful in the next stage. Bounds are inclusive: 0 and 100 are valid, −1 and 101 are not.

sections.title: A truth table without hidden execution
paragraphs: && is true only for true/true. || is false only for false/false. !true is false. A table of final values does not by itself show which operands were evaluated: built-in && skips the right operand after false, and built-in || skips it after true.
Zero converts to false and a nonzero number to true. Two is not a third logical value. Prefer domain conditions such as connected && !maintenance to unexplained numeric flags.

sections.title: Protection depends on the correct order
paragraphs: In divisor != 0 && 12 / divisor > 1 the divisor is checked first. At zero the left side is false, so division is skipped. Reversing the operands breaks protection by attempting division first. We discuss that unsafe reversal without executing it.

For ||, divisor == 0 || 12 / divisor > 1 protects the division. At zero the first condition is already true. Its meaning differs: no division is needed or the quotient is large. Safety does not make it equivalent to the previous && expression.

sections.title: Do not replace logical operators with bitwise ones
paragraphs: Single & and | are different operators and do not provide the same short-circuit protection. They may evaluate a dangerous right side. Use && and || for these guards. Full bitwise arithmetic comes later; for now understand why deleting one symbol changes the contract.
! has high precedence: !score == 0 does not mean !(score == 0). Use explicit parentheses when negating a condition, or assign a meaningful validScore name and use !validScore.

sections.title: Range validity and start policy
paragraphs: The laboratory first validates loadPercent within 0…100, then permits starting when connected and load is at most 80. Load 90 is a valid percentage but starting is forbidden. Separating valid from can_start distinguishes invalid data from a legitimate policy rejection.
Test −1, 0, 80, 81, 100, 101 and a separate disconnected case. Predict both flags. The short-circuit diagram explicitly names a skipped operand so meaning does not depend on color.

clarity.goal: Check a range with two conditions and distinguish “and” from “or”.
prerequisites: You know comparisons, bool and a range boundary.
model: A valid age in 0..120 means age>=0 AND age<=120. && is true only when both parts are true. || is true when at least one part is true. ! reverses truth and falsehood. Comparisons produce bool results.

&& and || evaluate their second part only when needed: a false first part settles && as false; a true first part settles || as true. This short-circuiting can protect division by checking its divisor first. This example only uses safe comparisons.

sections.title: Two boundaries need two comparisons
paragraphs: A score must be between 0 and 100 inclusive. In mathematics, 0 ≤ score ≤ 100 is convenient. The similar C++ expression compiles, but does not check what we intended.
Take score=120 and predict the results of 0 <= score <= 100 and score >= 0 && score <= 100. Follow the value that reaches the second comparison.

reveal.title: Compare your prediction and follow the steps
paragraphs: C++ 0 <= score <= 100 does not express two simultaneous bounds. First 0 <= score produces bool, which is then compared with 100. For the resulting 0 or 1, that second comparison is true even when score is invalid.

Check 0, 100 and 101 separately. They cannot share one expected answer: the first two are within the range and the third is not.
The program stores the intermediate bool in int firstComparison to make the conversion from true to 1 explicit. This is the same reason the chained comparison fails.

deep.title: Why does a truth table not show every executed operation?
deep.text: A truth table describes the result for two operand values. Built-in && may never evaluate the right operand when the left is false. That is what makes the divisor guard useful. This lesson concerns built-in operators on simple values, not user-defined operator overloads.
